title: Maghi at Muktsar
hookLine: the fair at Muktsar in January remembers the Forty Liberated

cards: The night before Maghi, Punjab lights bonfires. It's Lohri: people circle the fire, toss in sesame and popcorn, and sing. In some homes a pot of rice simmers slowly in sugarcane juice, to be eaten cold the next morning.
That morning is the first of the winter month of Magh. And in one Punjab town, Sri Muktsar Sahib, it's the day of a huge fair, with crowds walking in from the cold toward a pool.
You've already met the men that pool is named for.

teach.h: MAGHI — THE FIRST DAY OF MAGH.
teach.b: The fair is called Maghi because it falls on the first day of Magh, a winter month in the Punjabi calendar, usually in mid-January. Across Punjab it's a winter feast day. At Muktsar it's more.
On day ninety-one you heard why. Tradition says forty Sikhs left the besieged Guru and signed a paper saying they were no longer his Sikhs. Mai Bhago shamed them and rode back with them.
At the pool of Khidrana all forty fell, and Mahan Singh, dying, asked for the paper to be torn, and the Guru tore it. Today is how a town keeps that story.
Khidrana became Muktsar, the pool of liberation, and on Maghi the crowds come to that pool. People bathe in it, in January water, early in the day.
Then they go round the town's gurdwaras, each tied to a piece of the story. One is called Tuti Gandhi Sahib.
Tuti means broken; gandhi, tied. The broken, tied again. Tradition places it where the paper was torn.
Another, Shaheed Ganj, marks where the forty were cremated. There's kirtan, langar for whoever comes, and stalls and noise along the streets. It's a fair, after all.

teach.h: ONCE A YEAR, AND EVERY DAY.
teach.b: And the forty aren't remembered only once a year.
In the Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh worship, they're named every day: the Chali Mukte, the forty liberated ones. Look at what a whole town has chosen to remember. Not people who never left.
People who left, and came back anyway.

how: On Maghi, in mid-January, Sikhs gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib for a large fair, bathe in the sacred pool, and remember the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated, with kirtan, prayers and langar.

o: the winter feast day when Muktsar holds its fair
the bonfire night that ends the cold season
a summer fast day kept by the whole village

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: signed a paper and went home
where the broken bond was tied again

s: the Forty Liberated are honored because they never left
they did leave, and signed a paper saying so. they're honored because they came back.
Maghi falls on the first day of the month of Magh
a winter month in the Punjabi calendar, usually mid-January.
the forty are remembered only once a year, at Maghi
they're named in the Ardas every day: the Chali Mukte, the forty liberated ones.

games.q: it's Maghi morning at Muktsar, and it's cold. what do the crowds do at the pool the forty are named for?
o: stay away from the water until summer.
light a bonfire on its banks.
games.why: people bathe in the pool at Muktsar on Maghi, cold or not. the bonfires were the night before, at Lohri.

practice: Think of a place you go back to, not one you left in anger, just one you return to: a hometown street, a lake you swim in each summer, a grave you visit, a table where the same people gather every year.
See yourself arriving, and notice what has stayed the same and what has changed, including you. Stay a while with the coming back, and if you pray, hold that place and its people in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Maghi. The first day of the winter month of Magh, when the fair at Muktsar remembers the Forty Liberated.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: of Magh, the winter month; the day of the Muktsar fair.

carryVoice: Your line: come back, anyway. Coming back needs no speech, and neither does letting someone in. That's day one hundred fifty-three.
